## What we covered

How we measure whether a market is competitive, where that measure comes from,
and the problem that has to be solved before you can use it at all, which is
deciding what counts as the market. Then the trends in hospital concentration,
the policies that produced them, and the three kinds of merger.

## Key points

- The HHI is the sum of squared market shares, and it's easiest to understand
  from the two extremes. Five firms splitting the market equally is as
  competitive as five firms can be. One firm with essentially everything, and
  four that exist on paper, is as concentrated as it gets. Squaring the shares
  before adding them is what separates those two cases. Watch the scale: measure
  shares as decimals and the index runs up to 1, measure them as whole
  percentages and it runs up to 10,000, and you'll see both in practice. The
  thresholds are conventions rather than theory. Above 2,500 is highly
  concentrated, below 1,500 is unconcentrated, and the band between is moderately
  concentrated. Keep the vocabulary straight, because the two words run opposite
  each other: concentrated means uncompetitive. The reason a single number exists
  at all is that the DOJ and FTC see every proposed merger in every industry and
  can't investigate them all, so they need a filter that says which ones are
  worth a closer look. There is a theory behind it too, and knowing what the
  theory delivers tells you how far to trust the number. Take firms choosing
  quantities with the market price
  depending on total output, differentiate profit, and the markup over marginal
  cost as a share of price comes out as that firm's market share divided by the
  market demand elasticity. Call that the Lerner index, take the share-weighted
  average across firms, and the elasticity comes out front while the sum of
  squared market shares is what's left inside. So the HHI is the average markup
  in the market, scaled by the elasticity. You don't need to reproduce the
  derivation. You do need the conclusion and its price: this holds under strong
  assumptions, including homogeneous products, and in practice people use the HHI
  as a descriptive statistic the way they use a mean, without carrying the
  theoretical interpretation with it.
- Defining the market is where the whole argument happens, and it's easier to see
  outside health care. Suppose you're advising a grocery merger and want to argue
  the combined firm is small. You list competitors. Walmart, Publix, Costco,
  Sam's, Dollar General, the gas station that sells food, Amazon. Your share is
  tiny. Now switch sides and argue the combined firm is large. Costco sells
  everything, so it isn't a competitor. Whole Foods and Trader Joe's are a
  different product space. Narrow the set and the denominator shrinks and the same
  firm's share grows. Nothing about the firms changed. For a hospital it happens
  on two dimensions at once. In product space, I can claim a merger with an
  orthopedic hospital changes nothing because I do no orthopedics. In geographic
  space, draw Emory's market as its zip code and it has a hundred percent share,
  which is absurd because patients come from everywhere. Go up to the city and
  Gwinnett and Decatur and Sandy Springs are already outside it. Go up to the
  county and the same problem returns. Go far enough and you're counting people
  who drive from southern Tennessee. There's no principled stopping point, and
  the right one depends on the service, since the market for a gunshot wound is
  much smaller than the market for a transplant. The two defensible starting
  points are the hospital referral region, which you've seen already, and letting
  patient flows draw the boundary: walk out zip code by zip code, keep the ones
  whose patients mostly come to you, and stop where they mostly go somewhere else.
- Hospital markets have grown steadily more concentrated for decades, and it
  doesn't matter much how you define them. Mergers and closures both push the
  same way. Plot each market's index in 1990 against 2006 and almost every point
  sits above the forty-five degree line. On the metro-area data we looked at,
  Johnson City, Tennessee came in around 8,246, which is essentially one hospital
  system, and only about ten markets in the country sit below the 2,500 threshold
  at all, with St. Louis at roughly 2,527 near the bottom of the concentrated
  group. Atlanta is unusual in being somewhere in the middle. Being concentrated
  carries no extra regulation by itself. It only matters when a merger is
  proposed. Here's the sentence that ties this to the model we built: a hospital's
  outside option in a negotiation is its market power. Everything we've just
  described is that outside option rising for thirty years, which is the same
  thing as prices rising.
- Why it happened is mostly policy, not nature. For a long time the view was that
  competition among hospitals is wasteful. If you're a city paying for a hospital,
  a second one nearby means buying a second set of MRI machines to do the same
  work. And if you believe any bed you build will get filled, which is the
  supplier-induced demand argument in its bluntest form, then as a payer you
  limit beds to limit spending. That produced certificate-of-need laws, which
  require a would-be hospital to prove the community needs it before it can open.
  Many are still on the books. That's a barrier to entry, and it works. The
  consistency problem is the thing to take away: we chose a market to allocate
  health care and then spent decades suppressing the competition a market needs.
  You can argue for a different system, but that isn't the one we have. Meanwhile
  the evidence doesn't support the quality defense of consolidation. Mergers and
  closures don't improve care. If anything quality slips, usually on the patient
  experience side, communication and discharge instructions rather than mortality.
  Prices, on the other hand, go up reliably. Note the asymmetry in what we can
  study: entry is so rare in this industry that we mostly learn about competition
  by watching competitors disappear. One of these policies is worth knowing by
  name, since the discussion forum is about it. A certificate of public advantage
  lets a state approve a merger that would otherwise face federal antitrust
  scrutiny, on the condition that the state supervises the merged entity itself.
  The problem is what happens at the end. The certificate expires, the state
  oversight goes with it, and the merger does not come undone.
- Three kinds of merger, in descending order of how well we handle them.
  Within-market mergers are the well-understood case, and the price effects are
  large, routinely above twenty percent and sometimes fifty or sixty. A $15,000
  hip replacement becoming over $20,000. The effect is bigger the closer the two
  hospitals are, and the reason is the bargaining model again: if an insurer can
  send patients next door when it drops me, I'm weak, and once next door is mine
  the nearest alternative is far away. Prices at hospitals that weren't party to
  the merger rise too, since the whole market is more concentrated. These mergers
  are getting rarer mainly because systems are running out of local competitors to
  buy. Out-of-market mergers are now common, carry smaller but real price effects
  of five to ten percent, and are much harder to challenge, partly because the
  mechanism isn't obvious. If Emory buys a hospital in Tennessee, nothing about
  your choices in Atlanta changed. Two arguments explain it. Common customers:
  hospital markets are local but insurance markets aren't, so the employer and
  the insurer span both places even though no patient does. Multi-market contact,
  or mutual forbearance: if I meet you in many markets, I'll go easy on you where
  I'm strong so you go easy on me where you're strong, and we both price higher.
  That one came out of the airline literature. Vertical deals, hospitals buying
  physician practices and insurers buying hospitals and nursing facilities, go
  almost entirely unchallenged, because nobody has a model a court can apply.
  Prices still rise, through the same outside-option logic, since physicians I own
  don't refer outside my system. And treat the rescue story skeptically. The
  common claim is that these acquisitions save failing hospitals, and the data say
  the typical merger is between two large healthy systems.
